title: Machining & Cutting Fundamentals
summary: Material removal processes, cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut parameters, tooling, and surface finish control.

sections.heading: What Is Machining?
sections.content: **Machining** is the family of manufacturing processes that remove material to create a desired geometry: **turning** (lathe), **milling** (spindle-driven rotary cutter), **drilling**, **grinding**, and related processes. Unlike casting or forging, machining starts from stock and cuts away what is not needed — which is why it offers the best **accuracy and surface finish** of any manufacturing process, at the cost of material waste and cycle time.

sections.heading: The Three Cutting Parameters
sections.content:
Every machining operation is defined by three primary parameters:

1. **Cutting speed** $V_c$ (m/min) — the relative surface velocity between tool and workpiece:

$$N = \frac{1000 \times V_c}{\pi \times D}$$

2. **Feed** — for turning, feed per revolution $f$ (mm/rev); for milling, feed per tooth $f_z$ (mm/tooth), converted to table feed:

$$F = f_z \times z \times N$$

3. **Depth of cut** — axial $a_p$ and radial $a_e$ engagement into the material

Together they define the **Material Removal Rate** — the productivity measure:

$$MRR = a_p \times a_e \times f_z \times z \times N \quad [\text{mm}^3\text{/min}]$$

Higher $V_c$ and feed cut faster but wear the tool faster and degrade surface finish. Selection is a trade-off; see the interactive calculator below.

sections.heading: Key Conventional Processes
sections.content:
| Process | Machine | Motion | Typical Capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Turning** | Lathe | Workpiece rotates, tool feeds linearly | Cylinders, shafts, threads |
| **Milling** | Mill | Rotating cutter moves across work | Slots, pockets, faces, 3D surfaces |
| **Drilling** | Drill press / mill | Rotating drill feeds axially | Holes (then reaming/boring for accuracy) |
| **Grinding** | Grinder | Abrasive wheel, fine cuts | Hardened surfaces, Ra 0.4 µm and better |
| **EDM** | Spark erosion | Electrical discharges erode material | Hardened tooling, intricate cavities |

Choose by **geometry + material + tolerance**: mill for prismatic features, turn for rotational parts, grind for hardened steel and tight finishes, EDM where nothing else can reach.

sections.heading: Tool Materials & Geometry
sections.content:
Tool material selection governs the feasible cutting speed:

| Tool Material | Hardness | Max Practical Vc (steel) | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HSS** | High toughness | ~30-40 m/min | Drills, taps, form tools |
| **Carbide** | Very hard | ~120-250 m/min | The workhorse for milling/turning |
| **Ceramic** | Extremely hard | ~300-600 m/min | High-speed finishing of hard steels |
| **CBN / PCD** | Hardest | 1000+ m/min | Hardened steel, aluminum, composites |

Tool **geometry** (rake angle, relief angle, lead angle) controls chip flow, forces, and finish. Positive rake cuts more freely (better for soft/ductile materials); negative rake survives interrupted cuts and hard materials. **Inserted carbide tooling** (indexable inserts) replaced regrinding in most production — change the insert, keep the holder.

sections.heading: Chips, Coolant & Heat
sections.content:
Most of the cutting energy converts to **heat** at the shear zone — control it or it controls you:

- **Chip control** — continuous ribbons wrap around the tool and scratch the surface; chip breakers and correct feeds produce safe, short chips
- **Coolants** — flood emulsion (general), MQL/mist (light duty), high-pressure through-tool (deep holes, titanium)
- **Built-up edge (BUE)** — work material welding onto the cutting edge at low speeds on ductile metals; raise speed or use coated tools to avoid it
- **Tool wear** — flank wear and crater wear are normal; monitor and replace before catastrophic failure. A dull tool raises forces and ruins finish long before it breaks

sections.heading: Surface Finish & Tolerances
sections.content:
Machining's competitive advantage is **precision**. Practical capability:

| Process | Tolerance | Surface Roughness Ra |
|---|---|---|
| Rough milling/turning | ±0.1 mm | 3.2 - 6.3 µm |
| Finish milling/turning | ±0.025 mm | 0.8 - 1.6 µm |
| Grinding | ±0.005 mm | 0.2 - 0.8 µm |
| Honing / lapping | ±0.002 mm | 0.05 - 0.2 µm |

Surface finish and dimensional tolerance are linked — tighter tolerances need finer finishing passes and stable fixturing. Communicate critical features with [[gdnt-fundamentals|GD&T]] callouts so the operator and inspector know exactly what matters, and confirm achievable values with your machine shop before finalizing the drawing.

sections.heading: Interactive Cutting Parameters Calculator
sections.content: Compute spindle speed, table feed rate, and material removal rate for a milling operation. Select a workpiece material, enter the cutter and cutting parameters, and the tool calculates the values — the same math the [[cam-computer-aided-manufacturing|CAM]] software performs internally.

sections.heading: Machining Safety
sections.content:
Machining is unforgiving of shortcuts:

- **No gloves near rotating spindles** — they get pulled in, hands follow
- Remove **chips with brushes** — never bare hands or compressed air at the face
- Secure the workpiece — a part that moves under cut can become a projectile
- Use **proper eye protection** at all times
- Respect **tool-change and setup lockouts** — never reach into the machine while the program is running

keyTakeaways: Machining is defined by cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut — they jointly set MRR, tool life, and finish.
Spindle speed N = (1000 × Vc) / (π × D); table feed F = fz × z × N.
Match the tool material to the workpiece: carbide for production steels, CBN/PCD for hardened or abrasive materials.
Heat and chip control determine surface quality and tool life — coolant and chip breakers are not optional.
Define critical features with GD&T so machining and inspection target the same requirement.
